sentences: In 1934, on the twentieth anniversary of his death, the remaining relatives (all cousins) of a wealthy man are summoned to his mansion in a rural part of the country to view his filmed reading of his last will and testament.

Among them are a former surgeon; a flamboyant stuntman, who has forged a successful career in a faraway state; a noted English hunter; the hunter's female lover, also her cousin and roommate; the marginally successful American songwriter; and a rising fashion designer.
Overseeing the gathering is the wealthy man's lawyer, and his longtime maid who looks after the now-abandoned manor.
The wealthy man lets it be known in his reading how much he despised and loathed his kin by setting up a dogfight for the fortune and revealing that the designer is to be the sole beneficiary.
However, to claim the inheritance, the designer must spend the night in the house with the rest of the family and be deemed sane the next morning.
Should she be unable to, the wealthy man has a second reel of film in which he names the secondary heir.

As the group prepares to turn in for the evening, they are startled by the arrival of a psychiatrist at a nearby sanitarium who warns them that a deranged, disfigured patient who believes himself to be a cat has escaped from the institution.
The lawyer urges the others to keep the revelation from the designer for fear of frightening her, but the hunter breaks the news to her.
However, the designer seems unbothered.
The lawyer requests the designer meet her in the library, but the designer is startled when, while turned away from her, the lawyer vanishes behind a false bookcase.

The designer alerts the others about the incident, but each have varying levels of suspicion regarding her claims, especially when taking into account the family's history of mental illness and delusions.
The songwriter subsequently confides in the designer that he has discovered secret passageways beneath the mansion, and that he suspects the lawyer and the maid may be hiding something.
Later, the hunter supplies the designer with a gun for self-protection.
The songwriter and the designer subsequently locate a precious family heirloom—an extravagant gold necklace—in the house, frozen in a block of ice.
Later, when the designer falls asleep, the trenchcoat-clad killer enters her room through a trapdoor and steals the necklace from her throat, awakening and terrifying her in the process.
Her screams again alert the others, who rush to her bedroom.
The group is initially suspicious of the designer's claims, until the songwriter locates the trapdoor and, upon opening it, discover's the lawyer's corpse, her bloodied head wrapped in a pillowcase.
When the songwriter goes to explore the basement tunnels, he is struck on the head by the killer, but survives.
Shortly after, the hunter is murdered by the killer in the dining hall while trying to locate the wealthy man's second film reel.
While the songwriter also proceeds to search for the reel to uncover the identity of the secondary heir, the designer arms herself with the gun given to her by the hunter.
On the staircase, she is confronted by the killer, who wrestles the weapon from her before dragging her into a room in the basement.
A struggle ensues, during which the designer grabs at the killer's disfigured face and removes his rubber mask, showing the culprit to be the stuntman.
The stuntman reveals that he is the secondary heir to the wealthy man's fortune.
The psychiatrist appears, and the designer runs to him for safety, but he reveals himself to be aiding the stuntman.
The stuntman and the psychiatrist chain the designer to a medical chair in the basement.
The stuntman momentarily returns upstairs, where he is attacked by the songwriter and a fight ensues.
The maid hears the commotion, and enters the parlour, where she shoots the stuntman to death.

The songwriter and the maid then rush downstairs to save the designer, who is about to be mutilated and killed by the psychiatrist; they enter moments before he is about to stab her, and the songwriter shoots him dead.
At dawn, an ambulance arrives to remove the bodies, the former surgeon and the hunter's lover depart the mansion.
Meanwhile, the maid prepares tea for the designer and the songwriter as they proceed to view the wealthy man's second reel, in which he names the stuntman the second heir.
In August 1939, a motley group of travellers find themselves in a small hotel in a mountain region, awaiting a delayed train to a neighbouring country.
They include a "much-married madcap American heiress", and a wise-cracking American photographer.
That evening the heiress gets very drunk and is knocked unconscious.
The following morning, badly hungover, she finds herself in a train compartment with an elderly governess, and a German baroness with her servants.
Other travellers include two English gentlemen returning to their home country for a cricket test match, an English diplomat "larking about" with his mistress, and a doctor.
When the heiress wakes up, the governess has vanished.
Her fellow travellers, including the baroness, deny seeing the governess and declare that she never existed.
The heiress begins to doubt her own mental condition.
She starts to investigate, joined only by a sceptical photographer.
The train stops to pick up a badly burnt and heavily bandaged automobile accident victim.
Shortly thereafter, a "governess" apparently re-appears, but it is not her.
The train resumes its journey and the heiress is attacked.
The governess's broken glasses are found and the photographer now believes the heiress's story.
They surmise that the governess was lured to the baggage car and is being held captive — and that the heavily bandaged "accident victim" is in fact now the governess.
This proves to be the case and the doctor instructs his wife, dressed as a nun (with high heels), to drug their drinks, but his wife chooses not to do so.
At the next station the train is diverted onto a branch line and only the buffet car and one carriage are left.
The train stops and an officer of the regime's paramilitary corps (son of the governess's former employer), approaches the train, demanding that the governess be surrendered.
The passengers refuse and a gunfight ensues.
The governess chooses this moment to confess that she is in fact a courier with a vital coded message (she hums a tune to them) that must be delivered to a senior official in the capital.
She leaves the train and disappears.
The photographer and the two English gentlemen contrive to take over the engine and drive the train back to the main line and over the Swiss border.
Back in the capital at the foreign ministry, the duo attempts to remember the tune she sang, then suddenly they hear someone humming the same tune.
It is the governess who managed to escape her captors.
The nurse recounts, in a letter to her father, her mother's recent death, and details a job she has taken at an estate caring for the wealthy, elderly patient.
There, she is greeted by his butler, the manservant, and the lawyer, the patient's attorney.
She finds herself almost immediately drawn to a locked room on the second floor of the house.
She discovers that the recluse, the patient's mentally-challenged son, lives in the room.
The nurse develops a friendship with the patient, even confessing to him that her mother had been institutionalized and that her father had raped her mother.

Shortly after the nurse begins working at the estate, the patient's adult grandson the young man, who spent his life on a commune in a desert state, comes to stay after the accidental death of his parents.
After his arrival, a series of deaths begin to occur; the nurse and the patient discover his dog hanging from a tree in the garden.
The recluse also dies in what appears to be a suicide when he is found having jumped out the window of his room.
The young man makes sexual advances toward the nurse, who finds herself increasingly uncomfortable around him.

The manservant is murdered in the wine cellar, having been crushed under a fallen wine rack and clobbered with a table leg; the police, however, conclude his death an accident, though the lawyer accuses the young man of his murder.
Later in the evening, the house gardener, the groundsman, is confronted at the estate by the detective in a garage, who tells him the coroner has deemed the manservant's death a murder.
After he leaves, the groundsman hears a commotion behind him, and upon returning, he finds the detective dead.
The unseen killer also attacks the groundsman, beating him to death.
The nurse, while searching the house, discovers a bloodied table leg, and calls the lawyer, panicked.
He tells her he is on his way to the house.
Just as the lawyer arrives, she discovers the young man's body stuffed in a closet.

The lawyer confronts her, and tells her that he has just returned from the hospital where the nurse claimed her mother was kept, and reveals that her mother died during the nurse's birth; he also accuses her of the murders, telling her she had been institutionalized for murdering her father, who had molested her.
She then attacks the lawyer with the table leg, and storms downstairs to kill the patient.
However, the patient manages to knock her unconscious with a cane.
The film close as the nurse narrates her letter to her father, saying that maybe she will be able to return to the estate one day to take care of the patient.
At a city's beer festival, a veteran intelligence agency field agent and his team foil a microfilm transfer.
When the agent returns to the capital, his boss, the chief, reassigns him to a desk job because the agent did not arrest the rival spymaster, the head of the enemy agency in the region.
The agent explains to the chief that he knows how the rival spymaster thinks, and it would take time and resources to identify and learn about a new replacement.
The agent's good friend and protégé the younger man is nevertheless assigned to take over his mentor's old job.
Instead of accepting this situation, the agent takes action.
He shreds his personnel file and flies to a foreign city to visit his former lover the woman, whom he has not seen in a while.

The rival spymaster, guessing what has happened, meets the agent and invites him to defect to the enemy agency; when the agent refuses, the rival spymaster sarcastically asks if the agent will be retiring and writing his memoirs.
On the spot, the agent decides to do exactly that; write and publish a memoir exposing the dirty tricks and general incompetence of the chief's intelligence agency.
The woman is horrified, saying that the chief will send agents to kill him.

She nevertheless helps by mailing copies of the agent's first chapter to spy chiefs in his own country, the rival superpower, an eastern power, a continental country, another continental country and the island nation.
The chief assigns the younger man to stop the agent.
The rival spymaster, not wanting his own agency's follies exposed, also pursues his old adversary.
The agent baits his pursuers by sending them explosive chapters and by periodically informing them of his location.
Leaving the region, he returns to his own country, cheerfully renting the chief's unoccupied southern family home, where he writes more chapters.
After purposely leaking his address, the agent convinces the federal police (which has jurisdiction) to barrage the chief's home with both bullets and tear gas, to the chief's great dismay.
The agent flies to an island by chartered seaplane, then to the foreign capital to present his publisher with the final chapter.
The rival spymaster informs the younger man that one of his agents has spotted the agent in the foreign capital by chance.
The agent purchases a vintage biplane—a foreign-built version of a classic trainer—and hires an engineer to custom-modify it for a specific task.
The chief meets the agent's publisher, who rebuffs his threatening bluster and then tells them where the agent's hotel room is.
At the vacated room, all the pursuers read copies of the final chapter he has left for them.
The agent ambushes the younger man in his hotel room, ties him up, gags him, and informs the younger man that he will be flying across the strait from a small airfield near a coastal headland.
Meanwhile, the woman gives her intelligence agency minders the slip, and crosses the strait by hovercraft to rendezvous early the next morning with the agent.
While everyone converges on the airfield, the agent suffers a flat tire on his way and is taken by the local police to their station.
When a policeman recognizes him from a posted fugitive bulletin, the agent escapes by short-circuiting an electrical socket and stealing a police car.
The agent reaches the airfield, and the Americans and the rival spymaster arrive by helicopter soon afterward.
The agent's biplane takes off and is pursued by the chief in the helicopter.
The agent's biplane evades the chief's gunfire for a while, but the plane finally appears to be hit and suddenly explodes over the strait.
In fact, it was deliberately destroyed by the agent, who has been operating it from the ground by remote control.
The chief and his intelligence agency team assume that the agent is finally dead; however, the younger man wryly remarks that he "better stay dead".
Meanwhile, the agent sneaks away from a deteriorating building on the edge of the airfield and disposes of the remote control that he used to fly and destroy the biplane.
He and the woman set out for a few weeks' stay in the south of the continental country.
Months later, the agent's explosive memoir entitled after a children's game has become an international bestseller.

Disguised as a Sikh, the agent begins to chat in a British accent with a local bookstore clerk as he purchases a copy of his own book, much to the woman's complete exasperation with his antics and "ridiculous disguises".
The film is set in 1953 in the small community, the English village where the elderly sleuth resides.
A major film production company arrives to film a costume drama about two rival queens with two famous movie stars, the star and the co-star.
The star is making a much-heralded comeback after a prolonged career absence (due to a mental health crisis after her son was born with severe brain damage).
She and her husband, the filmmaker, the film's director, arrive with an entourage.
The star is angry upon learning that her rival the co-star is in the film.
The co-star and her husband, a businessman, the film's producer, soon arrive.
The villagers attend a village fête at the hall, a large manor house, to welcome the film crew.
During the indoor reception, the co-star and the star exchange insults while posing for photos.
A devoted fan, the local woman, bores the star with a detailed story about once meeting her during the war.
She recounts leaving her sickbed to meet the glamorous star.
The star asks the filmmaker to bring both her and the local woman a cocktail.
The local woman suddenly dies after drinking it.
Her death is later attributed to a barbiturate overdose in the drink, though is believed that the star was the intended murder victim.
She receives anonymous death threats made from newspaper clippings, and her coffee on the film set, which she refused to drink, was spiked with arsenic.
The inspector, the national police detective investigating the case is baffled.
He asks his aunt, the elderly sleuth, for help.
The elderly sleuth is recovering at home after injuring her foot at the village fête.
The suspects are the secretary, the filmmaker's assistant who is secretly in love with him and would like the star out of the way, and the hotheaded actress, the co-star.
The main suspect, the secretary, calls the murderer from a village phone box, threatening to expose them.
She is then killed by a lethal nasal spray containing prussic acid instead of hay-fever medication.
The elderly sleuth, now recovered, visits the hall and inspects the murder scene.
Helped by information that the young helper, her cleaning woman who was a server at the reception, has provided, the elderly sleuth solves the mystery.
However, another death has occurred at the hall that reveals the killer's identity: the star, who has apparently committed suicide.
The elderly sleuth explains that the local woman's story was the star's motive.
Years before, when the local woman sneaked out to meet the star, she unintentionally infected the star with German measles, a mild disease that can be dangerous for a pregnant woman's foetus.
The star's child was born mentally handicapped.
Hearing the local woman cheerfully recount their earlier encounter, enraged and overwhelmed the star who poisoned her.
She then made it appear that she was the intended victim, crafting the false clues.
The secretary, who called various suspects from a phone box, accidentally guessed correctly, prompting the star to murder her.
The filmmaker confesses to the elderly sleuth that he had poisoned his wife's hot chocolate to save her from being prosecuted, but the drink was untouched.
The star is nonetheless found dead, seemingly having poisoned herself.
One rainy night in a coastal city, after leaving a hotel, the witness's car breaks down on a side road during a rainstorm.
He sees a large car draw up a little way behind him.
A man throws something into a garbage can.
At first, the witness thinks nothing of it and proceeds to meet his best friend, a disabled war veteran, at a bar.
The following day, a young woman is found murdered in a garbage can, and the witness becomes a suspect.
At the city's annual heritage parade, the witness sees a local tycoon.
The tycoon, whom he recognizes as the man he saw at the garbage can.
The veteran begins to take an interest in the case.
His interest soon becomes a conspiracy theory that develops into an investigation with a skeptical witness and the bereaved woman, the dead girl's sister, along for the ride.
The three of them recklessly share their conversation at a restaurant where the tycoon's wife overhears them accusing her husband of murder.
The witness romances the troubled woman, the veteran's wife, who is suffering with alcoholism and depression.
After the veteran attempts to blackmail the tycoon as a way of making the tycoon incriminate himself, the veteran's house mysteriously burns down with the troubled woman inside.
After the fire destroys the veteran's house, he becomes convinced that the tycoon had been trying to kill the witness, but the witness worries that the troubled woman killed herself.
There are also shots throughout the film of a gas heater that might have been the cause of an accidental fire.
The businessman, who considers the tycoon a friend and mentor, warns the witness that the veteran is putting himself in danger and should leave the tycoon alone.
Now homeless, the veteran stays in the businessman's guesthouse, where he researches the tycoon.

He concludes that the tycoon was responsible for the death of the businessman's father years earlier in order to gain control of the marina, and that the tycoon later paid for the businessman's education and helped establish his business to maintain influence over him.
He thinks that the tycoon has also murdered the dead girl and the troubled woman.
The veteran takes an invitation the businessman received to a party at the tycoon's house and gets the witness to drive him there.
When the veteran tells the witness that he plans to kill the tycoon, the witness follows him.
After being spotted by the tycoon's wife and apprehended by security guards, the witness winds up in the tycoon's office.
The tycoon, a war veteran himself, sympathizes with the veteran and offers to talk with him personally.
After stealing one of the tycoon's horses, the veteran suddenly crashes through the window on horseback.
As the veteran lies dying from his injuries, the witness accuses the tycoon of killing the girl, and the tycoon responds ambiguously.
The witness steadies the veteran's gun in the veteran's hand and fires as the film cuts to black.
A big-city janitor is an avid fan of a television news reporter.
Another janitor, the co-worker, is fired from the same office building the janitor works at after a confrontation with the businessman, a wealthy Vietnamese man suspected of criminal connections.
Trying to have the co-worker reinstated, the janitor talks to the businessman.
However, he quickly realizes that the co-worker was fired for being disrespectful, most probably because of the xenophobic sentiments he developed while fighting in the war overseas.
One night, the janitor finds the businessman strangled to death.
Looking for the killer, the police become suspicious of the co-worker but also of the janitor, who fought overseas as well and was the first to find the body.
The co-worker lies to the police about where he was that night and later shows up with more money than he ever had.
Because of all of this, the janitor is sure the co-worker killed the businessman.
Meanwhile, the reporter believes the janitor knows something about the crime.
She keeps after him for information, a pursuit the janitor allows because he is romantically interested in the reporter.
The two start meeting regularly and soon develop feelings for each other.
One night, before one of their "dates", the businessman's Vietnamese associates attempt to kidnap her to know how much she has learned about their organization.
To escape them, the reporter manages to jump out of their car and onto the street, where the janitor picks her up on his motorcycle.
At the janitor's place, he takes care of her wounds, and the two eventually sleep together.
The co-worker is later revealed to be innocent of the murder; he lied to the police because he was secretly dealing with loan sharks from two different sides of town.
From them, he got two huge loans to start a business with the janitor, who refuses to be involved.
Worried about the co-worker's life, the janitor tells him to return the money.
The suitor, the reporter's fiancé, also suspects the janitor knows more than he lets on.
One night, he attempts to kill the janitor by strangling him.
However, the suitor fails this time and is forced to flee.
He turns out to be the murderer of the businessman, whose organization was helping the suitor smuggle out Jews from a foreign power.
When the businessman appeared with threats of blackmail, the suitor was forced to kill him.
Unaware of all of this, the reporter decides to break up with the janitor and marry the suitor, who belongs to her social class and, thus, would make her parents happy.
In an attempt to save his relationship, the janitor agrees to a meeting with her and her parents at the reporter's place.
However, before it occurs, the suitor calls the janitor pretending to be the reporter's father and talks him into going alone to a different address.
When the janitor does not show up at her place, the reporter goes to his apartment, realizes what is going on and calls the police.
Meanwhile, the janitor goes to the address the suitor gave him, which turns out to be a horse stable on a deserted street.
There, he is attacked by the suitor and an associate.
Using his knowledge of animals and a firecracker, the janitor creates a stampede within the building that ends up disarming the suitor and making his associate flee.
The suitor and the janitor fight hand to hand until the police arrive.
The suitor then stops fighting and goes outside.
One of the officers, the lieutenant, believes the suitor is armed (the suitor deliberately reaches into an inside pocket to give that impression) and shoots him dead.
Later, the reporter arrives and embraces the janitor, realizing he is alive and well.
A patient of a big-city psychoanalyst is murdered after a session, stabbed while wearing a raincoat belonging to the doctor.
Police detectives, the first detective and the second detective, investigate.
The first detective bitterly resents the doctor from a previous case in which the psychoanalyst's testimony led to a cop killer being institutionalized rather than sent to prison.
The patient's personal problems are in question until the psychoanalyst's secretary is also found brutally murdered.
The psychoanalyst realizes he is the murderer's target, while the two detectives treat him as their prime suspect.
A widower, the psychoanalyst expresses concern to his physician brother-in-law about the cops' behavior.
The first detective in particular is so aggressive in his interrogations, the second detective reports him to a superior and gets the first detective thrown off the case.
Posing as doormen, two gunmen break into the psychoanalyst's apartment.
He holds them off until the brother-in-law and two paramedics arrive.
Not trusting the cops, the psychoanalyst instead made an emergency call to the hospital for help.
Choosing a name out of the phone directory at random, the psychoanalyst hires an old, quirky private investigator who lives in a rundown apartment filled with clocks and cats.
The investigator saves his life by finding a bomb planted in the psychoanalyst's car.
After he reports this latest attempt on his life, the second detective promises to lend the psychoanalyst a more sympathetic ear than his partner had.
The first detective, however, has secretly cut a deal with their captain to keep an eye on the case from a distance.
One evening, the investigator phones the psychoanalyst and claims to know the killer's true identity, but refuses to reveal it over the phone because nobody can be trusted, not even the police.
He tells the psychoanalyst to meet him after midnight at the city pier and mentions a mysterious name.
But when the psychoanalyst and the second detective arrive, they find the murdered body of the investigator, holding a cuckoo clock.
After doing some research, the psychoanalyst realizes that the mysterious name is an Italian code name for the head of an organized crime syndicate.
Offering to hide the psychoanalyst in a safe house, the second detective instead drives him to a countryside mansion where the phony doormen appear.
The second detective draws a gun but points it at the psychoanalyst, telling him he trusted the wrong cop.
The psychoanalyst is taken to a crime boss, discovering that the mobster's wife is someone he knows, a quiet woman who has been seeing the psychoanalyst as a patient.
The crime boss feels he simply can't have anyone knowing his private business, despite the fact that the mobster's wife told the psychiatrist practically nothing during their sessions.
The psychoanalyst is taken to a warehouse to be done away with permanently.
The second detective, expecting a payoff, is killed instead.

The psychoanalyst tries to escape but is quickly re-captured, then beaten savagely by the crime boss until the first detective and a team of cops arrive just in time, having been called by the mobster's wife.
The crime boss is killed and the rest of his men are arrested.
At a cemetery where the psychoanalyst goes to visit his wife's grave once a week, the mobster's wife turns up to apologize for causing the psychoanalyst all this trouble at the cost of so many lives.
He has quit his private practice, so she asks if that means he can see a former patient socially.
It does and they begin to leave the cemetery together, but the mobster's wife is shot and killed by a mob sniper.
The actress, a washed-up, alcoholic actress who performs under a stage name, wakes up on Thanksgiving 1986 next to the bloodied corpse of a sleazy photographer in his big-city loft.
Suffering a hangover, the actress does not recall any events from the night before.
She phones her husband the hairdresser, a salon owner from whom she is separated, and he insists that the actress call the police.
Instead, she attempts to flee the city but is unable to get a flight amidst the crush of holiday travelers.
In a parking garage, she manages to hitch a ride back downtown from the ex-cop, a former police officer who was discharged.
The actress returns to the photographer's apartment to clean the evidence and obtain the murder weapon.
While leaving, she is met by the ex-cop, returning the pocketbook she left in his car; he claims to have tracked her to the area using a matchbook with the photographer's studio address on it.
The actress reluctantly agrees to invite the ex-cop into her apartment, where the two have a makeshift Thanksgiving dinner.
The evening ends with the actress drunkenly stumbling into bed, after which the ex-cop leaves.
In the morning, the actress awakens to find the photographer's dead body in her shower, causing her to flee her apartment.
She is met by the ex-cop, who is returning to check on her.
Suffering withdrawals, the ex-cop brings the actress to a convenience store to purchase beer, and she confesses to him the events that occurred the day before.

Believing the actress killed the photographer, the ex-cop urges her to contact the authorities, but she fears she will not be believed based on a domestic assault conviction in which she stabbed her ex-husband with a paring knife while intoxicated.
The actress visits her friend the performer, a drag queen, to obtain clothing to disguise herself.
The ex-cop subsequently confronts the actress, informing her that he searched her apartment but found no sign of the photographer's body, and believes that she may have been framed.
Meanwhile, police investigating the photographer's murder visit the hairdresser's salon to question him about the actress's whereabouts.
The actress spends the night at the ex-cop's home, and the two have sex.
In the morning, the actress is dismayed to find newspaper articles detailing her disappearance and suspicion in the photographer's murder.
She visits her lawyer, the attorney, who is overseeing her divorce case from the hairdresser.
Meanwhile, the ex-cop interviews the photographer's neighbor, who tells him she witnessed the actress raving in a drunken state the night of the photographer's murder.
The actress arrives at the hairdresser's salon, and he agrees to style her hair in attempt to further conceal her identity.
The actress stays at the hairdresser's salon while he attends a dinner with his new lover, the socialite, and is startled when the ex-cop appears there.
The hairdresser returns with the socialite and renders the ex-cop unconscious by bludgeoning him with a vase.
It is revealed that the socialite murdered the photographer, who had been blackmailing her with lascivious photographs, and the hairdresser framed the actress for the crime to protect her.
The hairdresser attempts to drown the actress in a bathtub to silence her, while a remorseful socialite looks on.
However, the ex-cop comes to and he shoots and wounds the hairdresser before losing consciousness again, thereby saving the actress.
Police arrive and the socialite turns on the hairdresser, telling police he is the one who murdered the photographer.
Later, the actress visits the ex-cop while he recovers in the hospital, and tells him she has not had a drink in two days.
The ex-cop reveals to the actress that he too is a recovering alcoholic.
When the ex-cop asks the actress to leave, she initially complies, before returning to his bedside and declaring that he makes her happy.
In 1955 in a big city, a client contacts a private investigator to track down a crooner, known professionally by a stage name.
The singer suffered neurological trauma resulting from injuries received in the war.
His incapacity disrupted a contract with the client regarding unspecified collateral.
The client believes that a private hospital where the singer was receiving radical psychiatric treatment for shell shock has falsified records.
At the hospital, the investigator discovers that the records showing the singer's transfer were indeed falsified by a physician.
After the investigator breaks into his home, the physician admits that he was bribed years before by a man and woman so that the two could abscond with the disfigured singer.
Believing that the physician is withholding information, the investigator locks him in his bedroom, forcing him to suffer withdrawal from a morphine addiction.
Hours later, he finds that the physician has apparently died by suicide with a gunshot to the eye.
A reluctant investigator agrees to continue the search when the client offers him more money.
He discovers that the singer had a wealthy fiancée, but had also begun another affair.
The investigator travels to a southern city and meets with the fiancée, who says that the singer is dead, or at least dead in her mind.
The mistress, the singer's lover, died years before but is survived by her 17-year-old daughter, who was conceived during the affair.
The daughter has a young light-skinned son of approximately three years old, and claims that she does not remember who fathered the boy.
The investigator tracks down the musician, a guitarist and former bandmate of the singer.
After the investigator uses force to try to extract details of the singer's last known whereabouts, the musician refers him back to the fiancée.
The following morning, police detectives inform the investigator that the musician has been murdered by suffocation; his penis severed and stuffed down his throat.
The investigator returns to the fiancée's home and finds her murdered; her heart removed with a ceremonial knife.
He is subsequently attacked by enforcers of the magnate—a powerful southern patriarch and the fiancée's father—who tell him to leave town.
The investigator finds the daughter at his hotel.
He invites her into his room, where they have sex, during which the investigator has visions of blood dripping from the ceiling and splashing around the room.
He soon confronts the magnate in a gumbo hut.
The magnate reveals that he and the fiancée were the ones who took the singer from the hospital.
The singer was actually a powerful occultist who sold his soul to the devil in exchange for stardom.
He got his stardom but sought to renege on the bargain.

To do so, he kidnapped a young soldier from the city's main square who was his exact age and strongly resembled him, and performed a satanic ritual on the boy, murdering him and eating his still-beating heart to steal his soul.
The singer planned to assume the soldier's identity, but he was sent overseas and suffered a severe war injury.
He was sent to the hospital for treatment of facial trauma and amnesia.
After taking him from the hospital, the magnate and the fiancée left him at the city's main square on New Year's Eve 1943 (the date on the falsified hospital records).
While hearing the magnate's story, the investigator runs into the bathroom, vomits and continually asks for the soldier's identity.
The magnate says that the soldier's dog tags were sealed in a vase.
He returns to find the magnate drowned in a cauldron of boiling gumbo.
At the fiancée's home, the investigator finds the vase containing the soldier's dog tag—stamped with the investigator's own name.
The investigator realizes that he and the singer are actually the same person.
The client, whose name is a homophone for a name of the devil, suddenly appears.
His true nature revealed, the client proclaims that he can now claim what is his: the singer's soul.
The investigator insists that he knows who he is, but his repressed memories of killing the physician, the musician, the magnate, the fiancée and the daughter eventually come flooding back.
The investigator returns to his hotel room, where the police have found the daughter murdered by gunshot, the barrel of the investigator's gun still inside her vagina, and his dog tags on her body.
